text:
Executive summary

This Place Delivery Agreement (PDA) is dated 18 November 2026. It strengthens the relationship between West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA), Homes England (HE) (the trading name for the Homes and Communities Agency), and the National Housing Bank (NHB), through an enhanced single delivery framework to accelerate housing delivery, unlock regeneration and underpin the vision of the WMCA Growth Plan to transform productivity across the region.

Building on the success of the existing Strategic Place Partnership (SPP), this Agreement represents a step change in the way the 3 organisations work together. It moves beyond collaboration towards co-delivery, bringing together local leadership, national expertise and investment capability behind a shared set of priorities.

This Agreement represents an enhanced model of place-based delivery. By combining local leadership, devolved influence, dedicated delivery capability, aligned investment and stronger accountability, WMCA, Homes England and the National Housing Bank will work together to deliver more homes, unlock regeneration, attract investment and drive long-term economic growth across the region.

Through this Agreement, the partners commit to:

accelerating social and affordable housing delivery — supporting the delivery of the mayoral ambition to increase the supply of social and affordable homes across the region and maximising the impact of the £1.7 billion Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) indicative spend amount

delivering WMCA’s most significant growth and regeneration opportunities — supporting delivery in regeneration zones and spatial priorities including estate regeneration and developing the regional housing and regeneration pipeline

putting housing investment decisions closer to place — aligning SAHP investment decisions and coordinating investment pipeline development with regional priorities, strengthening WMCA’s influence over housing delivery

unlocking investment and delivery capability at scale — mobilising public and private capital while strengthening the region’s ability to deliver complex projects

establishing a Joint Delivery Unit (JDU) — creating a single delivery structure bringing together WMCA, Homes England and National Housing Bank expertise, investment and delivery capability, under nominated co-directors from WMCA and Homes England

strengthening accountability and governance — providing clear routes for decision-making and escalation, ensuring barriers to delivery can be addressed rapidly and jointly by WMCA, Homes England and National Housing Bank, with day-to-day responsibility for the delivery of the Agreement being held by the Homes England Executive Director for the Midlands

creating effective collaboration — ensuring clear and effective governance arrangements between the local authorities, WMCA and Homes England

Commencement and term

This PDA shall commence on the date it is signed and shall continue for an initial period of 3 years (subject to an annual review) and shall thereafter continue for such further period or periods as shall be agreed in writing between the parties, provided always that any party may give not less than 90 days prior written notice to the others to terminate this PDA at any time.

1. Strategic context: West Midlands Combined Authority’s growth ambitions

Place overview

1.1 The WMCA area is the UK’s second-largest city-region economy, comprising:

Birmingham

Coventry

Wolverhampton

Dudley

Sandwell

Solihull

Walsall

It is home to a young, diverse and growing population, with a £77 billion economy that plays a nationally significant role in driving innovation and investment.

1.2 The region has a distinctive identity built on its industrial heritage as the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution, alongside modern strengths in advanced manufacturing, automotive production, clean technologies, health innovation, digital industries and financial services. Strategically located at the heart of the UK, the West Midlands benefits from excellent national connectivity, significant transport investment including High Speed Two (HS2), and strong research and innovation assets through its universities and business clusters.

1.3 Whilst the region faces challenges including high levels of derelict and underutilised brownfield land, viability constraints and increasing affordable housing demand, it also has substantial opportunities for growth through regeneration, housing delivery, and infrastructure investment. Through targeted public and private sector intervention, greater alignment between available resources, and strengthened partnership working, the West Midlands could unlock transformational placemaking and regeneration.

Housing and regeneration in the region

1.4 The West Midlands Growth Plan sets out a 10-year vision to raise living standards by growing a more productive, inclusive and sustainable economy, with benefits shared across all communities in the region. The plan focuses on 4 priorities:

empowering people

increasing business productivity

creating prosperous and resilient places

strengthening the region’s story and partnerships to attract investment and opportunity

Its ambition is to grow the economy by £17.4 billion, support 93,000 more people into work, deliver around 12,200 new homes annually, and put the West Midlands on a pathway to becoming carbon neutral by 2041. These ambitions can be achieved through a series of interventions, including but not limited to:

increasing housing supply — by targeting the delivery of around 12,200 new homes per year to meet population growth and support economic expansion across the region, supported by a regional Spatial Development Strategy and devolved housing funds

unlocking strategic development sites — through investment in infrastructure, transport and regeneration, particularly in locations with the greatest potential to support jobs and growth

linking housing delivery to economic growth — ensuring new homes support business investment, labour market participation and the creation of productive, sustainable communities

regenerating towns and cities — bringing forward brownfield development and creating attractive places where people want to live, work and invest

improving connectivity and infrastructure — integrating housing growth with public transport, energy networks and digital infrastructure to create well-connected neighbourhoods

supporting inclusive growth — ensuring that housing development contributes to improved living standards, reduced deprivation and greater opportunities for residents across all parts of the West Midlands

1.5 The Growth Plan is also supported by the ‘Homes for Everyone’ pledges that have been set by the Mayor of the West Midlands, Richard Parker, including:

building social and affordable homes and creating vibrant communities so that everyone can have a place to call home

unlocking the delivery of an extra 20,000 homes in the region by 2031

unlocking the delivery of at least 2,000 social and affordable homes annually, by 2028

Barriers to delivery

1.6 There are a range of barriers that the JDU will work together to address. These include:

economic and market conditions impacting delivery — the economic uncertainty and changing regulatory environment of the past few years have resulted in significant challenges for the house building industry, including build cost inflation, material and skills shortages, increased labour costs and the rising cost of debt

high levels of derelict, vacant or underutilised brownfield land — many strategic sites require remediation, land assembly and site preparation before development can be brought forward, increasing costs and complexities

significant viability constraints across pipeline sites — high abnormal costs associated with remediation, site preparation and infrastructure can affect the financial viability of housing schemes. In many regeneration areas, these costs are not reflected in the end values, resulting in suppressed land values and limited developer returns. This can stall or delay a site from being brought forward without public sector intervention

desirable density and, or, development type — the WMCA’s strategy is to facilitate higher densities of development in some locations, for example, town and city centres and at transport hubs (medium and high-rise development (multi-family) tends to attract lower values than low-rise (single family) which can exacerbate the viability gap and this situation is worsening with values for multi-family falling significantly since March 2026)

requirements for infrastructure investment — new places and communities need sufficient infrastructure and utilities provision, a lack of which hinders development. Providing the necessary infrastructure – new roads, public transport, high-quality public realm, energy and digital capacity – is expensive and time-consuming, and options for public intervention for such improvements are often limited

fund flexibility — available public funding and investment is currently delivered via a range of separate funds which can hinder the JDU’s ability to address the scale of regeneration needed across the region (blended funding approaches, prioritisation and the leveraging of private sector investment, alongside strengthened and improved devolved resources for future investment, are required to maximise impact)

capacity and capability — resource constraints can limit the ability to identify, develop and progress complex regeneration projects at pace, especially where the private sector is not yet involved in the development (we need to build the capacity of regional and local authorities to develop and progress priority regeneration sites)

co-ordination — successful delivery requires collaboration between local authorities, government agencies, infrastructure providers, developers and investors to overcome barriers and unlock sites

Strategic opportunities

1.7 Whilst the WMCA area has considerable challenges when delivering housing and regeneration, there are significant thematic opportunities that can be unlocked through the West Midlands PDA. These include:

social and affordable housing delivery — the delivery of social and affordable housing is a key priority for the region and increasing the supply of affordable homes ensures that the benefits of regeneration and economic growth are accessible to a wider range of residents and communities (priorities include increased Social Rent provision, larger family homes and estate regeneration)

town and city-centre redevelopment — many town and city centres across the region are undergoing redevelopment to respond to changing retail patterns and this presents opportunities to repurpose underutilised land and buildings, create mixed-use developments and enhance the attractiveness and vitality of centres as places to live, work and visit

estate regeneration — this will provide opportunities to improve the quality, density and sustainability of existing housing areas through redevelopment, refurbishment and placemaking interventions and there is a need to strengthen the public-sector approach, so that existing or new resources can be used to unlock delivery

infrastructure-led development — investment in transport, utilities, energy, digital connectivity and community infrastructure can unlock strategic development sites that would otherwise remain stalled (infrastructure-led development is a key mechanism to bringing forward housing growth, improving accessibility and creating sustainable, well-connected communities and this also enables residential developments to build on the significant transport and connectivity opportunities available to the region, including High Speed Two (HS2), Metro extensions and urban extensions)

regeneration zones and spatial priorities — focusing investment into strategic growth locations, regeneration corridors and areas with significant brownfield development opportunities enables the region to concentrate resources in priority areas, support economic growth and maximise housing delivery (for example, the Mayoral Development Corporation, supported by the wider Development Zone, will bring together planning, land and investment powers in East Birmingham to unlock major regeneration and infrastructure projects)

2. Going further, faster, and rewiring the state

2.1 The West Midlands Strategic Place Partnership, established in March 2024, marked an important step in strengthening collaboration between WMCA and Homes England around shared place-making and housing delivery objectives. Since its inception, the partnership has leveraged joint investment and targeted interventions to unlock more than 4,000 homes, with affordable housing accounting for over half of total delivery and including significant Social Rent provision.

2.2 The partnership has helped to unlock a diverse portfolio of projects including:

large-scale brownfield regeneration sites such as Digbeth High Street in Birmingham and Spon End Phase 1, Coventry

smaller and more specialist housing schemes including Hollyhedge Lane in Walsall and Royal Quarter in Wolverhampton

new development in strategic city centre locations, such as Stone Yard in Birmingham, Smithgate in Wolverhampton; and City Centre South in Coventry

2.3 Alongside these capital funding interventions, Homes England and WMCA have deployed a series of revenue funds to support local authorities with the pre-development costs associated with their priority housing pipelines. This funding continues to be used to progress stalled or delayed pipeline projects in preparation for upcoming funding years.

2.4 All partners now recognise we need to go much further, much faster, and show how we are rewiring the state to better serve the WMCA region. The PDA represents the next evolution of the Strategic Place Partnership, moving beyond collaboration towards co-delivery.

2.5 Together, the partners will establish a new model of place-based delivery capable of accelerating housing delivery, unlocking regeneration opportunities and supporting sustainable economic growth across the region. The JDU, operating under the strategic leadership of the Mayor and WMCA, will provide a single delivery framework through which strategic ambition can be translated into investable propositions, faster decision-making and tangible delivery outcomes.

2.6 The PDA recognises the important role of local authorities in delivering the housing, regeneration and placemaking needs of the region and will use the supporting Delivery Plan to set out the roles and responsibilities of all partners in relation to this agreement.

2.7 Regional delivery capacity across local authorities is being co-ordinated by WMCA, to enable a priority focus and WMCA to provide strategic capabilities that will align with the JDU.

Place Delivery Agreement: a new strategic framework to serve places and local leaders

2.8 The PDA sets out a single framework through which the WMCA, Homes England and the National Housing Bank will align resources, expertise, capacity, investment and delivery activity to accelerate housing delivery, unlock regeneration opportunities and support the growth ambitions of the region.

2.9 The Agreement concentrates on a focused number of delivery priorities where a co-ordinated approach can have the greatest impact in overcoming barriers to delivery, attracting investment and bringing forward transformational housing and regeneration outcomes. These priorities reflect the shared ambition of both organisations to use housing, regeneration and place-based investment as a catalyst for economic growth, productivity and inclusive prosperity. More broadly, partners will maintain and enhance the existing Housing Pipeline which will guide the deployment of resources, specialist support and investment activity across the region.

2.10 The priorities set out in sections 3 to 7 will form the initial focus of activity under this Agreement. They will be reviewed periodically by the partners to ensure resources remain focused on the opportunities where joint intervention can deliver the greatest strategic impact.

2.11 Fundamentally, this framework is intended to ensure that local priorities, national and local capability and land, investment, powers and expertise are aligned around a common set of delivery objectives.

3. Theme A: Social and Affordable Housing delivery

3.1 Affordable housing is one of the clearest examples of how this PDA will bring decision-making, delivery capability and accountability closer to place.

3.2 Through this Agreement, the JDU will ensure affordable housing investment is aligned with WMCA and the Mayor’s priorities for growth, regeneration and housing delivery. By combining regional decision-making with dedicated delivery capability and specialist affordable housing expertise, the partnership will enable investment decisions to be shaped more directly by local priorities and delivery opportunities.

3.3 The WMCA has an indicative spend amount of £1.7 billion through the SAHP, creating a significant opportunity to accelerate social and affordable housing and council house delivery across the region. Through the JDU, partners will work together to maximise the impact of this investment, increase the pace and scale of delivery, and ensure affordable housing investment supports wider regeneration, economic growth and placemaking ambitions.

3.4 By working together with local authorities, developers and housing associations the parties will facilitate an increase in social homes and council house delivery alongside broader regeneration and economic growth outcomes.

3.5 We set out how this will work here.

a) SAHP decisions on Continuous Market Engagement (CME) will be delegated to the Regional SAHP joint team, within agreed thresholds, with the JDU providing the governance forum for approval to enable investment decisions to be locally led.

b) WMCA and the Mayor will be given full visibility of the SAHP pipeline data for the region. Through the JDU and enhanced governance, they will be included in the affordable housing pipeline review and CME assessment process, providing local insights and data to inform investment proposals.

c) The partnership will maintain and enhance the region’s Housing Pipeline, ensuring activity and investment are directed towards opportunities that can unlock or accelerate delivery, address housing need and contribute to the ambitions of the West Midlands Growth Plan and regional SAHP priorities.

d) The JDU will provide regular reports on SAHP performance across the region, including progress against the West Midlands SAHP priorities set out in SAHP 2026 to 2036: Strategic Priorities in Established Mayoral Strategic Authorities.

e) A clear pathway for investing in affordable and social housing opportunities will be established, aligning WMCA investment and SAHP resources to support regionally significant schemes from early-stage development through to delivery, ensuring a transparent and co-ordinated approach to unlocking priority sites across the region.

f) CME investment will be prioritised where it supports the delivery of affordable and social housing, particularly on schemes where WMCA grant funding is already being deployed to unlock development and achieve strategic housing objectives.

g) Where WMCA intends to commit funding to unlock a scheme, Homes England will prioritise any related CME funding applications to help provide greater delivery certainty for the project and enable WMCA to progress grant funding applications. Where WMCA intends to commit funding to unlock a scheme, Homes England will assess CME funding applications by a mutually agreed deadline reflective of the complexity of the bid.

h) The parties will continue to align their respective investment activities that support affordable housing delivery. The parties intend to map out, clarify and align their respective processes so that due diligence, assessment and decisions can be co-ordinated when possible. The intention is to maximise efficiencies and impact for both Homes England and WMCA and improve outcomes for the bid applicants and the communities where investment is being considered. Where appropriate a joint project will be created within the JDU to focus on this alignment of activity and will report back to the JDU governance teams.

i) WMCA and the Mayor will be involved in the assessment and decision-making process for further procurement rounds or extensions to existing Strategic Partnership allocations that affect the region.

j) A clearly defined escalation process will be established where members of the JDU cannot agree on a SAHP CME investment decision, with matters referred through the PDA and, or, JDU or respective governance structures for resolution through monthly governance arrangements.

k) The partnership will work with Registered Provider Strategic Partners operating within the SAHP to align investment plans and develop a co-ordinated pipeline of social and affordable housing opportunities across the region, supporting delivery of WMCA and the Mayor’s housing, regeneration and growth priorities.

3.6 Recognising the government’s ambition to significantly increase council house delivery, Homes England will explore with the WMCA ways to:

review the barriers to delivery of council housing and work collaboratively with local authorities to implement the preferred approaches including the potential to align with other thematic areas including land, industrialised construction and other forms of investment

bring empty homes back into use and other improvements to existing stock including where there are positive links to be made to other policy areas such as reduced use of temporary accommodation

4. Theme B: Housing and Regeneration Pipeline

4.1 The JDU will maintain and enhance a shared Regional Housing Pipeline that will inform joint investment and resourcing opportunities for WMCA and Homes England, ensuring that there is a deliverable programme of projects across the region. This will include:

investment-ready opportunities that are deliverable in the near-term

projects where co-development or the targeted application of expertise or enabling investment will unlock near-term delivery

strategic growth and regeneration opportunities that have the potential to deliver transformational change over a longer-term period

4.2 Through the partnership, both organisations will work together to identify and focus activity where aligned land, investment, delivery powers and expertise or market engagement can have the greatest impact in unlocking homes, growth and regeneration outcomes across the region.

4.3 Building on work already underway partners will explore a new approach to unlock the true social value of public sector land. This will test a more co-ordinated approach to identifying, assembling and unlocking public land opportunities across the region.

4.4 The JDU will work with local authorities and wider public sector partners to identify a portfolio of priority sites, explore barriers to delivery, and assess the potential for a longer-term public sector land programme that could accelerate housing delivery, regeneration and economic growth rather than individual site disposals and piecemeal development. The JDU’s resourcing, drawn from across public sector partners, will be shaped further by the identification of priority sites and the required skills, resourcing and interventions to unlock delivery.

5. Theme C: Regeneration Zones and spatial priorities

5.1 The West Midlands presents significant opportunities for housing growth, with many development sites situated within regeneration zones and strategic growth corridors that can unlock wider economic and place-based transformation. The JDU will target interventions into these strategic locations, particularly areas with significant brownfield land capacity, to enable the region to maximise housing delivery, whilst also supporting regeneration, economic growth and the creation of sustainable communities.

5.2 For example, the Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC), supported by the wider Development Zone (MDZ), will bring together planning, land and investment powers in East Birmingham to unlock major regeneration and infrastructure projects. Together, these initiatives represent one of Europe’s significant regeneration opportunities, with the potential to deliver over 20,000 homes alongside commercial investment and transport infrastructure that will drive long-term growth and transformation. The scale, complexity and strategic importance of this area will require a co-ordinated public and private sector approach that will be supported through the joint working arrangements enabled by the PDA.

5.3 A co-ordinated approach to placemaking and regeneration will also enable the PDA to build on the significant housing growth potential enabled through the region’s strong and growing transport network, including key regeneration opportunities located near HS2 stations and the Metro extension, and unlock the delivery of well-connected homes and higher density developments. Enhanced connectivity provides opportunities to deliver well-connected communities and support higher-density developments in sustainable locations. Some of the most significant housing growth opportunities are linked to transport-led regeneration, including at Arden Cross, Langley and Portersfield, where investment in infrastructure is helping to unlock development at scale.

5.4 Where WMCA is planning infrastructure enhancements, Homes England will work proactively with WMCA to identify and assess associated housing opportunities, including estimated housing delivery potential and indicative intervention requirements.

5.5 Four growth corridors identify some of the most significant growth and regeneration opportunities across the region, creating a strategic focus for considering future investment and interventions through the JDU.

Birmingham and North Solihull Gateway

A globally significant regeneration area that connects Birmingham City Centre with Solihull, leveraging HS2, Birmingham Airport and major transport improvement that will unlock large-scale transformation and economic growth. Key opportunities include:

Birmingham Knowledge Quarter

Digbeth Creative Quarter

Sport Quarter

Ladywood

Arden Cross

Coventry Growth Arc

A major regeneration and investment programme that combines commercial developments, housing and improved transport connectivity, building on Coventry’s strengths in advanced manufacturing, automotive, creative and smart energy. Key opportunities include City Centre South, City Centre North and the Coventry and Warwick Investment Zone.

Black Country Growth Corridor

A strategically important manufacturing and regeneration corridor, building on the Black Country’s expertise in advanced engineering, automotive supply chains, metals and advanced materials. Supported by major investment into transport infrastructure, including the Metro extension, this area will see significant mixed-use regeneration through sites such as West Bromwich Town Centre, Portersfield and Grove Lane.

Wolverhampton — Walsall Growth Cluster

A significant growth and regeneration area that combines city and town centre transformation with advanced manufacturing, logistics and innovation. The corridor presents major opportunities for residential-led developments with key sites including Smithgate, St George’s and Brewer’s Yard in Wolverhampton, alongside Waterside Point, Station Quarter in Walsall.

6. Theme D: Estate regeneration

6.1 Estate regeneration will play a critical role in meeting current and future housing need across the West Midlands. A number of existing housing estates will require comprehensive redevelopment to improve housing quality, increase housing supply and unlock wider placemaking outcomes for local communities, including schemes such as Ladywood, Druids Heath and Spon End.

6.2 The delivery of estate regeneration is complex and long term, requiring sustained collaboration between public and private sector partners. Successful programmes depend on the co-ordinated delivery of infrastructure, investment, land assembly, and development phasing.

6.3 The JDU will work together to develop bespoke funding and delivery strategies that respond to local conditions, reduce barriers to implementation and accelerate the delivery of high-quality homes. Through this co-ordinated approach, estate regeneration can unlock housing growth, improve place quality and create thriving communities that meet the needs of existing and future residents.

7. Theme E: Place-based investment and finance

7.1 Delivery of the region’s housing and regeneration ambitions will require investment at a scale that cannot be achieved through grant funding alone. Unlocking transformational opportunities across the region will depend on the ability to combine public and private capital, recycle investment over time and develop investable propositions capable of attracting long-term institutional funding.

7.2 The National Housing Bank, launched by Homes England in 2026, has been established to accelerate the delivery of new homes and mixed-use regeneration schemes through flexible public investment. Backed by up to £16 billion of debt, equity and guarantee products, the Bank is designed to work with national, regional and local partners to unlock housing delivery, crowd-in private capital and support the government’s ambition to deliver 1.5 million homes, whilst delivering a positive financial return for the Exchequer.

7.3 WMCA and Homes England share an ambition to use the PDA as a platform to develop innovative approaches to place-based investment, enhancing the existing regional housing pipeline of investable opportunities and increasing the scale of private capital investment into the region.

7.4 As part of this Agreement, the National Housing Bank will actively seek opportunities to amplify the region’s local investment fund supporting housing and regeneration ambition and the Mayor’s priorities to attract wider investment using its lending, equity or guarantee capacity. The National Housing Bank will support the development of a pipeline of investment opportunities capable of unlocking a significantly greater level of private and institutional capital investment over time, including from the National Housing Bank.

7.5 Partners will work together to identify and develop housing-led regeneration, infrastructure-enabled growth, mixed-use development and strategic land opportunities that have the potential to unlock significantly greater levels of private and institutional investment over time.

7.6 The partnership will seek to:

maintain and enhance the prioritised pipeline of investable housing and regeneration opportunities across the WMCA area

align National Housing Bank products and investment capabilities with WMCA and the Mayor’s growth and regeneration priorities

maximise the deployment of National Housing Bank products in the region through targeted promotion, advice and support to the sector

crowd-in institutional and private-sector capital alongside public investment

explore innovative approaches to land, infrastructure and development finance that accelerate delivery, and improve viability, and minimise grant funding requirement

establish the region as a national exemplar for place-based investment and housing-led economic growth

develop replicable investment models that can be applied across a wider pipeline of housing and regeneration opportunities

7.7 The WMCA’s allocation of the National Housing Delivery Fund will operate alongside National Housing Bank investment activity, helping to address barriers to delivery and develop the investable pipeline required to attract future bank support. Together, these funding streams have the potential to create a flexible source of capital to unlock strategic housing and regeneration priorities across the region.

7.8 By combining devolved funding, National Housing Bank investment and private capital, the WMCA will test a new model of place-based investment designed to accelerate delivery, improve viability and support long-term economic growth.

8. Framework for delivery, governance, and implementation

8.1 This new single framework will help to strengthen local capability to support delivery, while recognising a desire to go further in boosting the capacity, expertise and sharing of good practice across the public and private sector partners in the WMCA region via a focused programme of activity.

8.2 The JDU will provide greater visibility and accountability to WMCA and the Mayor, giving greater control, influence and resources needed to build the homes and places communities require and to hold partners to account for delivery.

8.3 WMCA, Homes England and the National Housing Bank commit to progressing a joint Delivery Plan outlining key tasks, milestones and resourcing commitments underpinned by a governance framework which delivers on the principles outlined in this PDA.

8.4 Homes England and WMCA will agree to share all relevant data between both organisations as required, so far as the parties are legally able to do so and will put in place any necessary reciprocal data-sharing agreements in preparation for financial year 2027 and 2028. This will support efficient joint working, ensure a consistent evidence base, and reduce the risk of funding applicants providing conflicting information to each organisation.

Partnership commitments

8.5 The parties commit to:

align resources around agreed priorities

maintain and enhance a shared strategic development and investment pipeline

jointly identify and resolve barriers

coordinate stakeholder engagement

share intelligence and investment planning

support delivery through a dedicated JDU

8.6 This PDA will operate on a three-year basis and will be reviewed annually to ensure it remains aligned with evolving national policy, regional and mayoral priorities, market conditions and delivery opportunities. The PDA is intended to provide a single framework while retaining sufficient flexibility to respond to changing circumstances and emerging priorities.

8.7 Delivery of the PDA will be supported through:

a rolling delivery programme maintained through the JDU, responding to WMCA and the Mayor’s regional priorities, interventions and opportunities requiring joint action

a detailed annual Delivery Plan, agreed following approval of the PDA, translating strategic priorities into specific actions, responsibilities, milestones and resource commitments

an annual review process to refresh delivery priorities, resource allocations and pipeline activity without requiring the full PDA to be renegotiated

regular monitoring and performance reporting through the governance and accountability arrangements within this PDA, enabling partners to track progress, identify emerging risks and agree corrective action where required

8.8 The parties acknowledge that successful delivery will require ongoing collaboration between Homes England, the National Housing Bank, WMCA and wider delivery partners including local authorities, government departments, infrastructure providers, registered providers, investors and other stakeholders.

Joint Delivery Unit

8.9 The JDU will provide a single delivery interface between WMCA, Homes England, and the National Housing Bank to drive implementation of agreed priorities through:

programme management

pipeline development

opportunity identification

investment co-ordination

risk management

performance monitoring

8.10 To resource the JDU, Homes England will commit an initial package of staff capacity that is equivalent to 5 full-time equivalent roles including executive leadership and technical resource, as well as flexible resource to meet demand. This will form part of the broader construct in relation to the regional capacity and collaborative working review that has been undertaken by WMCA, targeting resource and expertise to meet the needs of the region. The partners will work together to identify the skills and expertise needed to support the delivery of priority projects.

8.11 Provisional capacity and capability estimates have been used in formulating this agreement. These will be refined and confirmed in the follow-on Delivery Plan for both Homes England and WMCA. Indicative Homes England resources are set out here.

Homes England resourcing of the JDU

Oversight, accountability and place leadership

Senior leadership and accountability (ERD) — Leadership and sponsorship of PDAs within Homes England. Provides the strategic interface between local leaders and the agency, aligning national priorities with local ambitions, resolving barriers to delivery, and ensuring places can rapidly access the full breadth of agency capabilities.

Partnership management and place co-ordination

Partnership management and co-ordination (including diagnostics and skills commissioning) — Day-to-day partnership leadership. Develops strategic priorities with EMSA; coordinates development and delivery of associated delivery plans and pipelines; undertakes diagnostics; facilitates relationship brokerage between public and private sector partners (including different parts of government); and leads relevant workstreams as required.

Delivery support — Day-to-day working level support for the activities listed.

SAHP interface — Responsible for coordinating affordable housing investment via SAHP in the WMCA area.

National Housing Bank interface — Responsible for coordinating National Housing Bank activity in the WMCA area.

Pipeline and business development

Pipeline development — Provide cross-disciplinary expertise across both Homes England and the National Housing Bank, working closely with partnership leadership to identify, develop and progress pipeline projects. This includes applying technical expertise to identify opportunities, diagnose delivery challenges, engage and work collaboratively with partners and delivery bodies, and develop robust investment propositions across a range of funding and investment products, including those operated by WMCA.

Project delivery

Project delivery — Overall leadership and project-level support through the end-to-end development process, deploying expertise across strategic priorities and leveraging the full range of investment tools, interventions and products available to Homes England, the National Housing Bank and WMCA.

Land assembly, planning, enabling and disposal — Expertise related to strategically acquiring land, preparing it for development through de-risking and pre development interventions, and disposing of and managing delivery through partners, including through a master development approach.

Infrastructure planning, provision, and contract management — Expertise related to the financing, delivery and management of complex infrastructure projects.

Project funding and investment — Expertise related to identifying and structuring project funding requirements, and identifying suitable sources of funding and investment from Homes England, the National Housing Bank, EMSA and, or, other public and private sources.

Affordable housing delivery — Expertise related to structuring and, or, securing affordable housing provision aligned to local priorities – including through managing relationship with local affordable housing providers.

8.12 The JDU will be complemented by housing delivery expertise from across the wider agency shaped to develop products, schemes and initiatives as part of this thematic capability, including on:

social and affordable housing

National Housing Bank finance and product specialists

specialist technical capabilities

strategy, research and innovation capacity

8.13 In the first instance, the specialist capabilities that the JDU has access to are expected to comprise:

Advisory Team Large Application Sites (ATLAS) — specialist planning support

New Homes Accelerator

climate, environment and sustainability

design, masterplanning and placemaking

community engagement and social impact

strategic planning

Compulsory Purchase Order

estate management and contingent assets and liabilities

capital projects delivery

research and analysis including market engagement

economics

geospatial

commercial and procurement strategy

risk management

SME and complex development loans — National Housing Bank

equity and joint venture partnerships — National Housing Bank

guarantees – National Housing Bank

infrastructure loans – National Housing Bank

low interest loans – National Housing Bank

Governance and accountability

8.14 The Governance Framework will be developed further through the Delivery Plan and will include:

creating significantly enhanced accountability through a shared performance framework and direct reporting arrangements to WMCA

establishing strengthened oversight arrangements involving the Mayor, the chairs of Homes England and the National Housing Bank, and the chief executives of both organisations

introducing quarterly senior sponsor meetings to oversee delivery, resolve barriers and hold the partnership to account for agreed outcomes

providing regular update reports to WMCA’s Housing Steering Group and, where required, WMCA’s wider governance forums, that detail the progress being made to achieve the strategic objectives of the PDA and commitments set out in the Delivery Plan.

8.15 In recognition of the commitment to create an even more responsive and re-wired delivery body as outlined in the Housing Minister’s letter, and to bring decision-making and accountability closer to impacted communities, the parties will commit in parallel to review existing delegations, reporting and accountability frameworks. Communications and stakeholder engagement activity will similarly be reviewed within the same timeframe to maximise Homes England impact. Homes England will ensure information on planned activity within the WMCA area is shared in advance via the JDU.

Delivery Plan

8.16 The PDA will be supported by a detailed Delivery Plan which will provide the primary mechanism for coordinating delivery activity and monitoring progress against agreed commitments.

8.17 The Delivery Plan will:

translate the strategic priorities and commitments set out within this PDA into deliverable programmes, projects and interventions

set out key milestones, outputs, funding requirements, resource commitments and critical dependencies

set out key milestones, outputs, funding requirements, resource commitments including the initial commitments made by Homes England to the JDU, and critical dependencies

identify risks, constraints and barriers to delivery, together with proposed mitigation measures and required decisions

establish performance measures, success indicators and reporting arrangements

maintain a forward pipeline of opportunities and activities to support delivery of shared priorities

set out the roles and responsibilities of WMCA, Homes England and local authority partners in delivering the strategic objectives and priorities of this partnership

identify areas where additional collaboration, resourcing, investment, or intervention may be required to achieve agreed outcomes

8.18 Each partnership commitment included within the Delivery Plan will identify:

the agreed commitment or activity

the responsible organisation or organisations

a named lead owner

target completion or review dates

expected outputs and outcomes

success measures and monitoring arrangements

8.19 Following approval of the PDA, the partners will jointly prepare the initial Delivery Plan and maintain it as a live document throughout the life of the PDA.

8.20 The partners will agree:

the timetable for preparation and implementation of the Delivery Plan

the lead organisation responsible for coordinating drafting and updates

governance arrangements for review, endorsement and approval

the senior officers authorised to approve revisions and updates

reporting arrangements to support effective oversight and accountability

Review

8.21 This agreement will be reviewed annually, or as required in response to government policy or fiscal events. The review will be led by the JDU and overseen by the governance arrangements of the PDA, reporting to the Chief Executive of WMCA and Mayor, alongside the Chief Executive and Chair of Homes England.

8.22 The review process will enable WMCA and Homes England to strengthen the detail and structure of the PDA, through the agreement of additional principles that are aligned to current and upcoming regional and national priorities.

8.23 The review will:

assess progress against the commitments and success measures set out in the Delivery Plan

consider emerging opportunities, risks and policy developments

review resource requirements and delivery capacity

refresh the rolling programme of activity and priority projects

recommend amendments to the Delivery Plan where required

8.24 Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, changes arising through the annual review process will be managed through updates to the Delivery Plan and will not require the PDA itself to be redrafted or re-executed.

8.25 This approach will ensure that the PDA remains a stable long-term framework while enabling partners to adapt delivery activity in response to changing circumstances and opportunities.

1. Confidentiality

In this clause the following words and expressions have the following meaning:

Confidential Information means the terms of this PDA and all information whether oral or written (on whatever medium stored) relating to this PDA disclosed or made available, directly or indirectly by one party or its employees, officers, representatives or advisers to the other party or its employees, officers, representatives or advisers but excludes any information which:

at the time of such disclosure is, or subsequently becomes, publicly available;

at the time of such disclosure is, or subsequently becomes, available to the Recipient from a person who, to the Recipient’s knowledge, is not under any confidential obligation in respect of that information; or

has been independently acquired by a Party without breaching any of their respective obligations in this PDA.

Each Party recognises that under this PDA it may receive Confidential Information belonging to the other.

Each Party agrees to treat all Confidential Information belonging to the other as confidential and not to disclose such Confidential Information or any other confidential information relating to each other arising or coming to its attention in the course of this PDA to any third party without the prior written consent of the other Party and agrees not to use such Confidential Information for any purpose other than that for which it is supplied under this PDA.

The obligations of confidence referred to in Clause 1.3 shall not apply to any Confidential Information which:

is in, or which comes into, the public domain otherwise than by reason of a breach of this PDA or of any other duty of confidentiality relating to that information; or

is obtained from a third party without that third party being under an obligation (express or implied) to keep the information confidential; or

is lawfully in the possession of the other Party before the date of this PDA and in respect

of which that Party is not under an existing obligation of confidentiality; or

is independently developed without access to the Confidential Information of the other Party.

Each Party will be permitted to disclose Confidential Information to the extent that it is required to do so:

to enable the disclosing party to perform its obligations under this PDA; or

by any applicable law or by a court, arbitral or administrative tribunal in the course of proceedings before it including without limitation any requirement for disclosure under Freedom of Information Laws (as defined in clause 2) and the Parties acknowledge that any lists or schedules provided by it outlining Confidential Information are of indicative value only and that the other party may nevertheless be obliged to disclose such confidential information; or

by any regulatory body (including any investment exchange) acting in the course of proceedings before it or acting in the course of its duties; or

in order to give proper instructions to any professional adviser of that Party who also has an obligation to keep any such Confidential Information confidential.

The Parties shall ensure that all Confidential Information obtained from the other Party under or in connection with this PDA:-

is given only to such of its employees, professional advisors or consultants engaged to advise it in connection with this PDA as is strictly necessary for the performance of this PDA and only to the extent necessary for the performance of this PDA;

is treated as confidential and not disclosed (without Homes England’s prior written approval) or used by any such staff or professional advisors or consultants otherwise than for the purposes of this PDA and in all instances such third parties are subject to a signed confidentiality undertaking.

Notwithstanding any other provision of this PDA, nothing in this agreement shall prevent Homes England and WMCA:

disclosing any Confidential Information for the purpose of:

the examination and certification of its accounts; or

any examination pursuant to section 6(1) of the National Audit Act 1983 of the economy, efficiency and effectiveness with which Homes England has used its resources; or

disclosing any Confidential Information to any other department, office or agency of the Crown provided that in disclosing such Confidential Information pursuant to this paragraph (b), it discloses only the information which is necessary for the purpose concerned and requires that the information is treated in confidence.

publishing the Agreement to the general public in its entirety (but with any information, which is exempt from disclosure in accordance with the provisions of the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), redacted) and in the case of WMCA disclosing the terms of the Agreement to its constituent councils and non-constituent councils.

Save as otherwise set out in this clause 1, no Party shall, and each Party shall use reasonable endeavours to ensure that no contractor, officer, employee or agent shall, communicate with any representative of any press, television, radio or other communications media on any matter concerning this PDA without the other Party’s prior written consent (in each case, not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed).

2. Freedom of Information

In this clause the following words and expressions have the following meaning:

Freedom of Information Laws means the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 and any subordinate legislation made thereunder from time to time together with any guidance and/or codes of practice issued by the Information Commissioner in relation to such legislation;

The Parties are each a public authority as defined under the Freedom of Information Laws and so may be required to disclose information in response to a request for information under those laws (Request for Information). The Party in receipt of a Request for Information (Recipient) shall be responsible for determining whether any such information insofar as it relates to this Agreement should be disclosed pursuant to a Request for Information and will:

where appropriate and as soon as reasonably practicable inform the other Party that it has received a request to disclose information in response to a request for information under the Freedom of Information Laws; and

in relation to such information and pursuant to the Freedom of Information Laws, consider the application of the exceptions and exemptions to disclosure before complying with any obligation to disclose such information.

Nothing in this PDA will prevent any Party from complying with any valid order, decision, enforcement or practice recommendation notice issued to it by the Information Commissioner under the Freedom of Information Laws.

comply with all applicable laws, statutes, regulations, and codes relating to anti-bribery and anti-corruption including but not limited to the Bribery Act 2010 (Requirements);

not engage in any activity, practice or conduct which would constitute an offence under sections 1, 2 or 6 of the Bribery Act 2010 if such activity, practice or conduct had been carried out in the UK;

have and maintain in place throughout the term of this Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) its own policies and procedures, including but not limited to adequate procedures under the Bribery Act 2010, to ensure compliance with the Requirements, the Relevant Policies and paragraph (b), and will enforce them where appropriate;

The Parties shall ensure that any person who is performing services or providing goods in connection with this Agreement does so only on the basis of a written contract which imposes on and secures from such person obligations in the same terms as paragraphs (a) to (c) above and also an obligation to immediately report to the appointing party any request or demand for any undue financial or other advantage of any kind received by them in connection with the performance of such services or the provision of such goods and to (at the request of the appointing party) produce a written certificate confirming compliance with the anti-bribery requirements and to provide such supporting evidence of compliance as the appointing party may reasonably request.
